text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London ended firmer across the board but backed off earlier highs as New York's July contract failed to maintain upside momentum. August ended $3.60 higher at $316.90 per tonne, while October closed $2.40 higher at $305.40 per tonne.

According to trade sources there could be a nearby tightness of high quality white sugar as sugar from the European Union's new crop will not appear before September/October and traders have to rely on the tail-end of the current crop for their supplies.

However, the question is of course, whether there is a strong demand for high quality sugar. Raw sugar futures in New York closed sharply higher with front month July gaining 16 points to close at 11.04 cents/lb, while October added 17 points to close at 10.87 cents/lb. The strength was mainly technical although the increase in the US import quota contributed to the firmer tone. There still seems to be no fundamental basis for a strong rise in world market prices.

UNITED STATES - The United States Department of Agriculture increased the US import quota by 200,000 tonnes on May 12 in the final use this year of a formula that sets US import needs. Under the USDA formula, the quota goes up by 200,000 tonnes if the projected stocks-to-use ratio is 15.5 per cent or less.

In April USDA forecast a ratio of 14.4 per cent, compared to 14 per cent in March, when a 200,000 tonne increase was approved. In the estimate released on May 12, the USDA predicted a stocks-to-use ratio of 15.4 per cent so that the quota automatically went up by 200,000 tonnes. For fiscal 1997, USDA said it would use the stocks-to-use ratio to decide in January, March and May whether to allow more sugar into the country above the 1.7 mn tonnes allocated at the start of the fiscal year.

While the quota was increased by 200,000 tonnes in March and May, an increase was denied in January. Despite adopting the formula USDA retained the power to increase the quota if the need arises. Traders said a further increase may be necessary because demand is expected to strengthen in summer and autumn and flooding in the Red River Valley has slowed deliveries of beet sugar.

UNITED STATES - Sugar imports in February 1997 amounted to 290,834 tonnes, raw value, down from January's 354,747 tonnes but still considerably up on the 234,649 tonnes imported in February 1996. This brought cumulative imports in the first five months of 1996/97 (October/February) up to 1.124 mn tonnes against 677,928 tonnes in October/February 1995/96. Total imports in 1995/96 reached 2.615 mn tonnes against 1.558 mn tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of origin in October/February 1996/97 were Guatemala with 176,172 tonnes raws against 90,292 tonnes, Brazil with 134,626 tonnes, up from 96,743 tonnes and the Philippines with 122,869 tonnes compared to nil. Sugar exports in February 1997 dropped to 8,363 tonnes, down from 25,171 tonnes recorded for February 1996. This brought cumulative exports in October/February 1996/97 up to 76,137 tonnes compared to 158,112 tonnes in 1995/96. JAPAN - Sugar imports in March 1997 reached 69,821 tonnes, raw value, down from 87,677 tonnes in March 1996. This brought cumulative imports in the first half of 1996/97 (October/March) up to 752,206 tonnes against 814,453 tonnes in 1995/96. Total imports in 1995/96 amounted to 1.681 mn tonnes against 1.716 mn tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of origin in 1996/97 were Australia with 401,452 tonnes raws against 427,783 tonnes, Thailand with 172,793 tonnes, down from 252,146 tonnes and South Africa with 114,542 tonnes against 129,768 tonnes.
